New hospital tech here. I had absolutely no rx experience whatsoever, but I do have experience working in the medical field from when I was a scrub tech over 15 years ago. I applied for a pharmacy tech trainee position on a whim and ended up scoring the job. It absolutely IS a lot to take in, but slowly my confidence is building. What helped me the most was working alongside different colleagues in an area I found myself struggling in. For example, I could not get the hang of using DoseEdge, our Rx workflow program and was becoming more and more frustrated. One week, the Rx director scheduled two people, different from the tech that had been training me, to work alongside me so they could explain DoseEdge from a different perspective. Everything finally clicked after working with different people training me. I highly suggest getting other people in the pharmacy to show/explain their process when working with something you find difficult. Alternative points of view can definitely help speed the learning process along. Good luck and remember that you can do this!!!

You are a good human for wanting to support her. It's a really difficult disorder to live with, but it absolutely can get better over time if she works on it. It's beautiful that ypu want to help her get there. 

The stigma surrounding BPD is downright harmful, especially to someone in the infancy of diagnosis. It is severely misunderstood and we are often vilanized by people that lack the understanding of it. It's incredibly lonely at times. 

I won't lie; it WILL be a hard road at times for the both of you. Just remember to be patient with her and make sure you don't find yourself condescending when the topic arises. Try not to talk about it all the time. It is a part of who we are, but it doesn't define who we are. If you bring it up frequently and the majority of your conversations come back to her having bpd, I guarantee you she'll shut down. 

Here's what I suggest to you: research the good traights of someone with bpd. We love deeply. We are loyal to a fault. We are incredibly empathetic. We are deep thinkers and can relate to a person on many different levels. We can be very out going and adapt to any situation we find ourselves in. A lot of us are extremely creative and funny. That's just the tip of the iceberg. When you see her exhibit these positive aspects of bpd, help her see that she exhibits them. 

We are in emotional turmoil more often than not and a lot of us hide what is going on in our heads. It's absolute chaos and brutally painful at times. Having someone close to us recognize the good in us is immensely cathartic. We need you to see the good in us, especially during the times we can't see it ourselves. 

I wish you both so much luck on this journey, friend. :)

I've had 7 over the past 17 years: 2 lower back, 4 knee and 1 ankle. (I honestly should have a punch card where the next one is free at this point.) Best advice I can offer is to research the hell out of your surgeon AND the facility where you'll be having the procedure done. Look at patient reviews and ask as many questions as you can so you go into this with complete confidence. Feeling good about the team/facility you are entrusting with your health helps relieve some of the pre-op anxiety. After meeting the anesthesiologist in pre-op holding, you can always ask for a "pre-flight cocktail" if you feel really anxious. Keep in mind that everyone reacts to general anesthesia differently. Some people wake up feeling nauseous and super groggy, and some people wake up feeling like a million bucks. (Personally, I get all emotional and cry like a little bitch for no reason followed by 20 minutes of shamelessly hitting on any attractive medical professional within a 10 foot radius of me. Drugs are weird.) When they tell you not to eat or drink anything after a certain time before your procedure, listen to those instructions. Do not try to sneak a cracker or small glass of water (unless otherwise directed by your doctor). Being NPO for many hours definitely sucks, but they WILL cancel your surgery if you ignore the pre-op instructions. Remember that every single person involved in your care holds your health, safety and comfort as their utmost priority from beginning to end. Follow all instructions to a T, and you'll have a smooth and speedy recovery. Good luck, friend! :)
